papers.abstract: Hybrid retrieval, which fuses a sparse lexical retriever with a dense neural one, is widely recommended in the software documentation surveyed in September 2026, usually with reciprocal rank fusion (RRF), on the strength of aggregate gains. We ask what fusion costs on individual queries, treating "do not fuse" as a first-class outcome, in the setting in which hybrid retrieval is deployed: a standard Anserini BM25, five dense encoders spanning 22M-596M parameters and three model generations, a learned-sparse (SPLADE) alternative, and a cross-encoder second stage, on seven BEIR datasets and three fusion functions. Even the best method, dense-weighted score interpolation, ranks relevant documents below the better of its two components on 13-48% of queries and below the deployable dense-only retriever on 8-21%, while beating dense-only in aggregate on every corpus with the primary encoder; the downside is significant under loss-averse risk-sensitive evaluation on six of the seven corpora. We call this loss the fusion tax. It is mostly a ranking effect that preserves recall in aggregate, it is most likely on the queries that only one retriever covers, and it persists across the encoder ladder and the SPLADE substitution. RRF carries the higher tax wherever the dense retriever is clearly stronger and only beats dense-only where the two components are balanced. Fusion failure is weakly predictable within a corpus but transfers unreliably across corpora, because the features that predict it change sign with the sparse-dense balance. A cross-encoder recovers part of the tax only where it is itself reliable. We distill these findings into guidance that keys the fusion decision to the measured sparse-dense balance of the target corpus.

deep_reading.content:
Hybrid retrieval fuses the results of term-matching sparse retrieval such as BM25 with those of dense vector retrieval into a single ranking. The documentation of Elasticsearch, Azure AI Search and LangChain all list reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) as the recommended or only fusion method, on the basis of gains in average metrics. This paper keeps the books differently: it compares nDCG@10 before and after fusion query by query, and treats "no fusion" as a legitimate option. The authors test on 7 BEIR datasets with standard Anserini BM25 and the BGE-small dense model. The best fusion method is score interpolation with a 0.7 weight on the dense score, which beats dense-only retrieval in mean nDCG@10 on every dataset, by 0.008 to 0.051; yet in the same setting 8–21% of queries rank worse than with dense-only retrieval, and 13–48% rank worse than the better of the two retrievers on that query. The authors call this per-query loss the "fusion tax". ==The losses concentrate on queries where only one retriever finds a relevant document, and the other retriever then contributes only noise==. Switching to a larger dense encoder, replacing BM25 with SPLADE, or adding a cross-encoder reranker after fusion does not make this tax disappear.

## 1. The average went up, so why look query by query

A higher mean nDCG@10 only says that more queries were helped than hurt; it does not say that no query was hurt. For a RAG system the difference has practical consequences: if fusion pushes a query's relevant document out of the top 10, the context given to the generator no longer contains the answer, and the answer quality for that query drops directly, while the average does not show it.

The authors therefore keep two accounts for every query. The first uses the "per-query best" as reference: whichever of BM25 and dense retrieval does better on a given query is compared with the fused result. This reference is only known after the fact and measures whether fusion drags down the better retriever. The second uses "always dense-only" as reference, an alternative that can actually be deployed, and answers whether adding BM25 is worth it at all.

## 2. The accounting: one formula, four quadrants

The fusion tax of a single query is defined as the nDCG@10 of the better of the two retrievers minus the nDCG@10 after fusion:

$$\tau(q)=\max\big(\mathrm{NDCG}_s(q),\,\mathrm{NDCG}_d(q)\big)-\mathrm{NDCG}_f(q)$$

Here $s$ is sparse retrieval (BM25), $d$ is dense retrieval and $f$ is the fused result. $\tau(q)>0$ means fusion is worse than the better retriever on that query. The share of queries with $\tau>0$ is called the "oracle tax"; the share of queries where fusion falls below dense-only retrieval is called the "deployable tax".

Three fusion methods are compared. RRF sums the reciprocals of the ranks, with the constant set to 60. Score interpolation first min-max normalizes the scores of each retriever's top 100 (best score 1, worst 0), then adds them as $s_f=\alpha\tilde s_d+(1-\alpha)\tilde s_s$ with dense weight $\alpha=0.7$. The paper does not say how a document found in only one of the two top-100 lists gets its missing score; the usual choice is 0. CombMNZ sums the normalized scores and multiplies by the number of retrievers that returned the document.

To find where the losses come from, the authors split queries into four quadrants by whether each retriever puts at least one relevant document in its top 10: both retrievers hit (Both-Win), only dense retrieval hits (Dense-Only), only BM25 hits (Sparse-Only), and neither hits (Both-Fail).

![Each point is a query; the x-axis is BM25 nDCG@10 and the y-axis is BGE-small dense nDCG@10 (paper Figure 1). Colors compare the best of the three fusion methods with the better of the two arms: fusion more than 0.01 higher is green (helped), more than 0.01 lower is red (hurt), within 0.01 is grey. Look at where the red points sit: they cluster far from the diagonal, especially along the axes, that is, on queries where only one retriever works.](figs/2610.30612/fig1_quadrant_scatter.png)

The sparse side uses BM25 with Anserini default parameters (k1=0.9, b=0.4, title and body indexed as separate fields), which the authors confirm reproduces the published BEIR results to 4 decimal places; this rules out the explanation that "BM25 drags fusion down because it was badly tuned". The main experiments use BGE-small (33M parameters) on the dense side, with MiniLM (22M), BGE-base (110M), BGE-large (335M) and Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (596M) as alternatives, all searched exactly with FAISS. The 7 datasets are SciFact (scientific claim verification), FiQA (financial QA), NFCorpus (medical nutrition retrieval), TREC-COVID (COVID literature retrieval), ArguAna (finding counter-arguments), SciDocs (citation recommendation) and Quora (duplicate question retrieval), with query counts ranging from 50 for TREC-COVID to 10,000 for Quora.

## 3. Experiments

### 3.1 Averages: interpolation does win

This experiment first checks whether fusion is as effective on average metrics as is usually claimed. The authors compare nDCG@10 of each retriever alone and of the three fusion methods with BGE-small on the 7 datasets (paper Table V):

| Dataset | BM25 | Dense-only | RRF | Interpolation α=0.7 | CombMNZ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SciFact | 0.6647 | 0.7200 | 0.7152 | **0.7307** | 0.7230 |
| FiQA | 0.2361 | 0.3848 | 0.3667 | **0.4087** | 0.3872 |
| NFCorpus | 0.3254 | 0.3371 | 0.3570 | 0.3547 | **0.3574** |
| ArguAna | 0.4142 | 0.5950 | 0.5549 | **0.6027** | 0.5702 |
| SciDocs | 0.1581 | 0.1973 | 0.1954 | **0.2070** | 0.1976 |
| TREC-COVID | 0.6559 | 0.6660 | 0.8010 | 0.7166 | **0.8045** |
| Quora | 0.7886 | 0.8878 | 0.8695 | **0.8997** | 0.8857 |

Score interpolation beats dense-only retrieval on all 7 datasets. RRF beats dense-only retrieval only on NFCorpus and TREC-COVID, where BM25 and dense retrieval are at similar levels (0.656 vs 0.666 on TREC-COVID); on the other 5 datasets RRF is below dense-only retrieval. ==RRF looks only at ranks and not at scores, so even when dense retrieval is clearly stronger it treats BM25's ranks as equally trustworthy==, which dilutes the dense side's advantage.

### 3.2 Per-query accounts: how many queries get worse behind the higher average

This experiment checks how many queries are hurt, and how badly, while the average rises. The authors compare interpolation and RRF query by query against dense-only retrieval and against the per-query best (paper Table VIII):

| Dataset | Interp. worse than dense | Mean loss when worse | Interp. better than dense | Mean net change | Interp. below per-query best | RRF worse than dense |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SciFact | 10.0% | 0.205 | 14.7% | +0.0107 | 20.0% | 15.3% |
| FiQA | 14.7% | 0.100 | 23.1% | +0.0239 | 23.3% | 30.4% |
| NFCorpus | 18.3% | 0.044 | 33.4% | +0.0177 | 39.0% | 23.8% |
| ArguAna | 19.1% | 0.213 | 21.8% | +0.0077 | 30.4% | 32.9% |
| SciDocs | 20.9% | 0.070 | 26.1% | +0.0097 | 36.2% | 27.6% |
| TREC-COVID | 14.0% | 0.054 | 72.0% | +0.0506 | 48.0% | 26.0% |
| Quora | 8.2% | 0.167 | 12.4% | +0.0119 | 12.8% | 16.2% |

Take ArguAna: interpolation makes 19.1% of queries worse, the worsened queries drop by 0.213 on average, almost as much as the 0.221 average gain of the improved queries, and the mean net change is only +0.0077. ==The small rise in the average is the difference left after large gains and large losses across many queries cancel out==.

One might suspect that the 0.7 weight was picked on the test data. The authors re-select the weight with leave-one-dataset-out cross-validation: choose $\alpha$ on the other 6 datasets and apply it to the 7th. The resulting deployable tax is 11–25%, slightly higher than with a fixed 0.7, which shows the tax is not caused by tuning on the test set. The risk-sensitive test TRisk works query by query on the nDCG@10 change of fusion relative to dense-only retrieval: gains count as they are, losses are multiplied by $(1+\alpha)$ (the authors use $\alpha=5$), and the test asks whether this weighted mean is significantly below zero. By this standard, interpolation is significantly riskier than dense-only retrieval on 6 of the 7 datasets, even though its mean score is higher.

### 3.3 Which quadrant the losses come from

This experiment checks which kind of query the losses come from. The authors split interpolation's per-query gains and losses by the four quadrants of Section 2 (paper Table VII). Result: Sparse-Only queries make up no more than 7% of the total, but 87–95% of them are hurt by fusion, with mean net losses of 0.14 to 0.37 within the quadrant. The reason is that dense retrieval has no relevant document in its top 10 on these queries, and the 0.7 dense weight pushes down the relevant documents BM25 found. Dense-Only queries are the mirror case: BM25 becomes the noise source and 38–65% are hurt. Among Both-Win queries, 10–48% are reordered, with help and harm nearly cancelling and a quadrant net change between −0.04 and +0.01; because this quadrant holds the most queries, it contributes 38–72% of the worsened queries.

These losses come mainly from rank changes, not from relevant documents going missing. Queries whose top-10 recall actually drops are only 1–7%; in most cases the relevant documents are still in the top 10, just moved down a few places. Across all datasets, only 77 queries have all their relevant documents pushed out of the top ten, so the fusion tax is mainly worse ordering, not worse recall.

### 3.4 A bigger encoder does not remove the tax

![The x-axis is the parameter count of the dense encoder (log scale), the y-axis is the share of queries hurt by fusion (relative to the per-query best); left is interpolation, right is RRF (paper Figure 3). Follow the trend of each line: as the encoder grows from 22M to 596M, the share of hurt queries does not decline systematically.](figs/2610.30612/fig3_tax_vs_encoder.png)

This experiment checks whether the fusion tax exists only because the dense model is weak. The authors step the dense encoder up from 22M to 596M, then redo the experiment with BM25 replaced by the learned sparse retriever SPLADE. Result: with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, interpolation still puts 14–43% of queries below the per-query best; with SPLADE it is 14–41% on 6 datasets and 60% on TREC-COVID. ==A stronger encoder only changes the balance between the two retrievers, and that balance decides which retriever becomes noise on each query==, so the share of hurt queries does not decline as the encoder grows.

### 3.5 Can we tell in advance which queries should not be fused

If this could be predicted, queries could be routed: fuse where fusion helps and use dense-only retrieval elsewhere. This experiment checks whether that is feasible. The authors extract 17 features available at inference time for each query (query length, IDF statistics of its terms, the score gap between the first and second result of each retriever, the overlap of the two top-10 lists, and so on) and train gradient-boosted trees to predict whether fusion will fail. "Failure" means that on this query, fusion's nDCG@10 is more than 0.01 below the better of the two retrievers. Result: AUC is 0.63 within a dataset, falls to 0.59 across datasets, and is as low as 0.49, close to random; 11 of the 17 features flip the direction of their association with failure across datasets. A router built on these features does not beat fixed interpolation on any dataset. A concrete example is the dense side's score lead, the similarity gap between dense retrieval's first and second results: on datasets where dense retrieval is stronger it signals that fusion is safe, but on TREC-COVID it signals that fusion will fail.

### 3.6 Can reranking repair the damage

This experiment checks whether a cross-encoder reranker after fusion can repair the losses fusion causes. The authors rerank the top 30 with BGE-reranker-v2-m3. After reranking, the reference also becomes reranked dense-only retrieval, and the tax is the share of queries where fusion falls below it. This deployable tax falls by a third only on SciFact, and not at all on FiQA or TREC-COVID, where 16% and 22% of queries still finish below reranked dense-only. The reason is that reranking repairs old losses while creating new ones. Take FiQA: of the 95 queries fusion had hurt, reranking repairs 75, but newly hurts 81, so it gains nothing. After reranking, nDCG@10 barely differs (at most 0.011) whether the candidates come from interpolation or from dense-only retrieval, which means that with a reranker, the fusion step can largely be dropped. The cost is latency: cross-encoder reranking of 30 candidates takes about 1.6 s, while BM25 needs only a few milliseconds per query.

## 4. Limitations

The authors list five limitations: only retrieval ranking is evaluated, not the final answer generation; only one reranker and one reranking depth are tried; TREC-COVID has only 50 queries, so its percentages fluctuate a lot; latency is measured on one machine only; and the prediction experiment uses only cheap features, without trying LLM judgments.

Two further points deserve attention. First, all 7 datasets are English BEIR datasets whose queries are mostly natural-language questions, and dense retrieval is stronger than BM25 on all 7 of them; in keyword-heavy settings such as e-commerce or code search, Sparse-Only queries may be far more than 7%, and both the quadrant shares and the recommended weight need to be re-measured. Second, Section 3.3 shows that most of the loss is relevant documents moving down within the top 10; if the downstream system feeds all 10 documents into the generator's context, this loss affects the answer much less, which is exactly the gap left by not evaluating generation.

## 5. Practical implications

First, before adopting hybrid retrieval, measure the nDCG@10 of each retriever on the target corpus. The authors' advice is that if dense retrieval leads by more than 0.04, use dense-leaning score interpolation (dense weight 0.6–0.7); only when the two are close use RRF, CombMNZ or equal-weight interpolation. This call does not need much labeling; 200–400 queries are enough. The weights also carry over to other datasets: a weight chosen on the other 6 datasets scores at most 0.014 nDCG@10 below the weight tuned directly on that dataset (TREC-COVID is the exception, at 0.031), so there is no need to retune for every corpus.

Second, in online evaluation, report "the share of queries worse than dense-only retrieval" and "the mean loss when worse" alongside the average. These two numbers show directly whether a higher average comes from most queries gaining a little, or from some queries gaining a lot and cancelling out large losses on others.

Chunking schemes for RAG are almost always compared on one static corpus, yet the documents in a knowledge base keep changing. Each chunk is embedded on its own, so if an edit moves a chunk boundary, the chunks on either side become new embedding inputs even when not a single word in them changed. This 6-page short paper measures that update cost directly: the authors take 120 pairs of adjacent revisions of Chinese and English Wikipedia articles, allow an old vector to be reused only when a chunk's complete embedding input is byte-identical to one in the old version, and compare three chunking methods with a frozen BGE-M3 encoder. On the 116 articles where all three methods succeed, non-overlapping fixed-size chunking recomputes 57–68% of the new version's embedding input, paragraph-first recursive chunking 38–56%, and content-defined chunking (CDC) 43–54%; under a 2048-token retrieval budget, the three differ in evidence recall by less than 2 percentage points within each language. ==Fixed-size chunking shifts everything after the insertion point, so none of the downstream windows can match the old version, which is why it recomputes the most==. Which of recursive chunking and CDC is cheaper flips as the chunk-length parameters change.

## 1. Why measure update cost

An English article had only 0.13% of its text edited, yet fixed-size chunking recomputed 49% of its embedding input while paragraph-first chunking recomputed only 8%. This example from the paper's dataset shows that the amount edited and the amount recomputed can be far apart, and the gap is determined by the chunking rule.

For a knowledge base that is continually updated, the amount recomputed maps directly to embedding compute and to writes into the vector index. Earlier chunking evaluations only compared retrieval quality, but two schemes with similar retrieval quality can differ a lot in update cost: on the English articles in this paper, fixed-size chunking's mean recompute fraction is 1.5 times that of paragraph-first chunking (57% vs 38%). The authors want to answer three questions: how much each of the three chunking methods must recompute; whether that amount is driven by edit size, edit position or cut-point rules; and whether the scheme that recomputes less also retrieves worse.

## 2. Measurement

![Schematic drawn for this write-up, not to scale. The top half shows fixed-size windows: after a few sentences are inserted into paragraph 1, every window starting after the insertion point shifts, and all 4 windows must be re-embedded. The bottom half shows splitting by paragraphs or text fingerprints: cut points follow paragraph breaks or local content, the insertion affects only paragraph 1, and the 3 chunks after it reuse their old vectors unchanged.](figs/2610.31019/fig0_boundary_drift_schematic.png)

The reuse rule is strict: a chunk's complete embedding input (its text plus the encoder's special tokens) must be byte-identical to the input of some chunk in the old version for the old vector to be reused; a single differing character makes it a new input. The cache holds only the previous version of the same document and does not match across documents. The recompute fraction is defined as:

$$R_c=\frac{\sum_{x\in M_c}T(x)}{\sum_{x\in U_c(D_{\mathrm{new}})}T(x)}$$

Here $U_c(D_{\mathrm{new}})$ is the set of distinct embedding inputs that chunking method $c$ produces on the new version, $M_c$ is the part of it not found in the old version's cache, and $T(x)$ is the number of input tokens of chunk $x$. $R_c=0$ means everything is reused and $R_c=1$ means everything is recomputed. The authors also run a no-edit control: chunking the same version twice must give $R_c=0$, otherwise it counts as a pipeline failure.

All three chunking methods see only the current version and fixed parameters, never how the old version was chunked:

- Fixed-size chunking: greedily cuts non-overlapping windows of at most 304 tokens.
- Recursive chunking: splits any span longer than the 400-token target, preferring blank lines, then line breaks, then sentence-ending punctuation (Latin or full-width) followed by whitespace, and falls back to fixed windows only when none works; it then greedily packs the small units up to the target length.
- CDC: uses the Steadlith implementation, which computes Rabin rolling fingerprints over the word sequence (a hash of the few words in a sliding window) and places a cut wherever the hash meets a preset condition (the paper does not state it; the usual choice in such methods is that the low bits of the hash are all zero). Chunk lengths are limited to 176–352 tokens. The method was originally built for file-system deduplication; cut points depend only on nearby content, so inserting bytes near the front of a file does not move the cut points after it.

The chunk-length parameters of the three methods were tuned in advance so that their median chunk lengths are close (the actual maximum ratio is 1.17).

Retrieval quality is measured as follows: each article has two questions, 240 in total, and annotators mark on each version the character spans that answer the question. At retrieval time the candidate pool holds all articles collected in the same batch (the paper does not give the batch size): the article being asked about appears in the version under test, the others in their old version. Chunks are ranked by dot product, and whole chunks are packed into a 2048-token budget in rank order; recall is 1 if the packed chunks cover one complete evidence set.

## 3. Experiments

### 3.1 Main result: fixed-size chunking recomputes the most, recall differs little

This experiment answers how much each method must recompute and whether retrieval quality differs. The authors average the recompute fraction and evidence recall with fixed parameters over the 116 articles where all three methods succeed (paper Table I):

| Language | Chunking | Recompute fraction | Evidence recall | Median chunk length (tokens) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Chinese | Fixed-size | 68.4% | 97.4% | 304 |
| Chinese | Recursive | 55.7% | 98.3% | 356 |
| Chinese | CDC | 54.0% | 98.3% | 314 |
| English | Fixed-size | 57.4% | 96.7% | 304 |
| English | Recursive | 37.9% | 96.8% | 342 |
| English | CDC | 42.8% | 95.0% | 291 |

Paired by article, recursive chunking recomputes 12.7 percentage points less than fixed-size chunking (Chinese, 95% interval −19.7 to −6.2) and 19.6 points less (English); CDC recomputes 14.4 and 14.7 points less than fixed-size chunking. Paired differences in recall range from −1.9 to +0.9 points, with all intervals including or touching 0. The authors state explicitly that these intervals cannot rule out a drop in recall and do not prove equivalence, so they do not rank the methods by recall.

Recursive chunking's advantage is smaller in Chinese than in English because of its cut-point rules: Chinese sentence-ending punctuation is usually not followed by a space, so overly long Chinese paragraphs cannot be cut at sentence boundaries and fall back to fixed windows.

The smaller the edit, the larger the gap. On English articles with less than 5% edited, fixed-size chunking recomputes 46% of chunks on average, while recursive chunking and CDC need only about a quarter, because their cut points follow the content and an edit does not shift every later cut point. The Chinese articles follow the same pattern: fixed-size chunking recomputes over 60%, and CDC the least (36%). When more than half is edited, all three methods must recompute 60–90%, and at that point the choice of chunking no longer matters.

### 3.2 Edit position: why fixed-size chunking recomputes so much

![Mean recompute fraction of the three methods when 1% of text is inserted at the start, middle or end of 2 Chinese and 3 English development articles (paper Figure 3). Look at the blue line: fixed-size chunking recomputes everything for an insertion at the start, and less the later the insertion point; the orange and green lines stay below 30% at all three positions.](figs/2610.31019/fig3_insert_position.png)

This experiment tests whether "boundary shift" is the main source of recomputation. It changes only one variable: the same 1% insertion is placed at the start, middle or end of the article, with everything else unchanged. Result: fixed-size chunking falls from 100% for an insertion at the start to about 12% for one at the end, because every window after the insertion point moves back by the length of the insertion and no downstream chunk can be reused. Recursive chunking and CDC stay below 30% at all three positions, as paragraph breaks and content-fingerprint cut points realign quickly after the edit.

The authors also run a verbatim check: how much of the recomputed input is text that already exists unchanged in the old version. On English articles, 50% of the tokens fixed-size chunking recomputes are text present verbatim in the old version, 33% for CDC and 12% for recursive chunking (47%, 45% and 37% in Chinese). ==This text was not changed at all; it was only cut into different chunks, so recomputing it is caused entirely by the cut-point rule==.

### 3.3 Whether recursive chunking or CDC is cheaper depends on parameters

This experiment checks whether the ranking of the two content-aware methods is stable. Without retuning, the authors try 6 target chunk lengths between 256 and 496 tokens for each method and compare paired settings whose median-length ratio is at most 1.15. Result: the CDC-minus-recursive recompute difference ranges from −2.4 to +6.2 points in English and from −0.7 to +5.5 in Chinese, flipping sign in both languages. For example, in English raising recursive chunking's target length from 400 to 448 raises its recompute fraction from 37.9% to 46.2%, while CDC at the same 448 is 43.8%. The reason is that recursive chunking packs several small paragraphs into one chunk; once an edit changes one paragraph's length, the packing of several following paragraphs can change too, and the larger the target length, the farther this chain reaction propagates. Fixed-size chunking recomputes the most in every setting.

The authors checked the cost once more on the arXivEdits paper-revision data: the mean recompute fractions of fixed-size, recursive and CDC chunking are 94.5%, 81.4% and 80.2%, with fixed-size still highest. The text-extraction noise of this dataset is unquantified, so it serves only as side evidence on cost.

### 3.4 Overlapping windows are not the fix

A common remedy is to let adjacent fixed windows overlap by 32 or 64 tokens. The result is a recompute fraction within 1.3 points of the non-overlapping version, 10–26% more total embedding input, and English recall down by 3.0 and 3.9 points, because the duplicated text uses up the 2048-token retrieval budget.

## 4. Limitations

The authors list these limitations. Wikipedia is the only source. The annotations of the 240 questions were not independently adjudicated by multiple people. The revision pairs were collected in three rounds (the first two inspected by hand, the larger third filtered automatically and checked twice by a model). When an author re-checked a stratified sample of 60 labels from the second and third rounds, 57 matched the original annotation, and the 3 mismatches were all questions labeled unanswerable whose versions actually contained relevant information. The median chunk-length ratio of the three methods is 1.17, above the preset 1.15; only one encoder is used; and the related method KARA was not run. KARA keeps the previous version's chunk layout, builds a graph over candidate cut points and picks the shortest path that reuses the most old chunks; it is built for incremental updates, so without it we do not know how much further such methods could cut recomputation. CDC failed on 4 Chinese articles because CDC splits words on spaces, so a long run of Chinese text without spaces is treated as a single unit of 403–550 tokens, exceeding the 352 maximum.

Two further points deserve attention. First, all three methods recovered all the evidence in 105 of the 116 articles, and recall is generally above 95%, close to the ceiling, so this retrieval setup cannot distinguish small quality differences between methods. Second, the recompute fraction measures embedding input and is not converted into latency or cost; if embedding is a small part of the whole update pipeline, for example when index rebuilding or review costs more, a gap of a few tens of percentage points is diluted in the total cost.

## 5. Practical implications

First, if a knowledge base is edited often and in small amounts, do not use non-overlapping fixed-size chunking. Switching to paragraph-first recursive chunking takes the mean recompute fraction on English articles from 57% to 38%, and from 46% to 25% on small-edit articles, with retrieval recall essentially unchanged. The precondition is to use the byte-identical input as the cache key, so that vectors are reused whenever the text has not changed.

Second, when evaluating chunking schemes, report the recompute fraction together with retrieval quality, and measure both under your own chunk-length parameters. The ranking of recursive chunking and CDC flips with parameters, so no ranking in the paper can be carried over as is. For Chinese corpora, check whether the cut-point rules rely on spaces; otherwise recursive chunking falls back to fixed windows and CDC fails outright.

papers.title: Lean Finder V2: Semantic Search for Mathlib That Disambiguates User Queries
papers.authors: Jialin Lu, Xiaoyu Liu, Hengrui Luo, Rodrigo Stehling, Linxi Liu, Weiran Sun, Yuepeng Wang, Wuyang Chen
papers.summary: People writing proofs and coding agents alike must first find suitable theorems in Mathlib, the mathematics library of the Lean proof assistant. Real search queries are short, they leave out much of the intent, and the same phrase may correspond to several similar theorems. Lean Finder V2 tackles the problem from both ends. On the model side, the authors use reinforcement learning to train a query generator that writes, for each theorem, short queries the current retriever ranks poorly but whose meaning still matches. These queries train the retriever, the new retriever then scores the generator, and the two alternate for two rounds. On the input side, the authors automatically optimize a rewriting prompt: candidate prompts rewrite a batch of synthetic queries, the retriever's rank for the target theorem is checked, and only versions that improve the rank are kept. Before retrieval, it rewrites the user's short query. On MathlibQR, made up of human-written short queries, Lean Finder V2 reaches Recall@10 of 0.893, against 0.780 for the previous best retriever-plus-reranker system.
papers.abstract: We introduce Lean Finder V2, a semantic search framework for Mathlib that disambiguates user queries through complementary model-level adversarial training and input-level query rewriting. Human mathematicians and coding agents rarely search Mathlib by providing detailed context. In practice, they query short properties, notation, aliases, or hypotheses, leaving much of the intended mathematics implicit. In contrast, existing Mathlib search engines unrealistically assume context-rich queries. The scarcity of real-world short queries paired with ground-truth Mathlib statements makes this ambiguity even more intractable. We argue that this is essentially a data problem. Through adversarial training, we scale up the generation of labeled short and ambiguous queries, and learn to disambiguate user queries at both model-level fine-tuning and input-level query rewriting. On the human-curated MathlibQR benchmark, our Lean Finder V2 sets a new state of the art, with at least 11% relative improvement over the previous best Mathlib semantic search engines. On top of our state-of-the-art retriever, optimized query rewriting further improves MathlibQR retrieval. On unlabeled queries from human and coding-agent interactions, Lean Finder V2 is ranked as the strongest system. Integrated with Claude Code, Lean Finder V2 improves proof success on downstream theorem-proving task.

Real search queries are short: the median length of human-written queries is 16 tokens and of agent-written queries 15, while the natural-language paraphrases of theorems used to train earlier retrievers have a median length of 82 tokens. Short queries leave out much of the intent, and the same phrase may correspond to several similar theorems. Lean Finder V2 tackles the problem from both ends. On the model side, the authors use reinforcement learning to train a query generator that writes, for each theorem, short queries the current retriever ranks poorly but whose meaning still matches; these queries train the retriever, the new retriever then scores the generator, and the two alternate for two rounds, producing more than 600,000 query–theorem pairs. On the input side, the authors use GEPA to automatically optimize a rewriting prompt that makes the user's short query more explicit before retrieval. On MathlibQR, made up of 810 human-written short queries, Lean Finder V2 reaches Recall@10 of 0.893, against 0.780 for the previous best retriever-plus-reranker system. ==In the ablation, rewarding only "hard" without checking whether the query and theorem agree makes the top-rank metrics worse than using no synthetic data at all, because the generator learns to write off-target queries to manufacture difficulty==.

## 1. Why short queries are hard to search

![Paper Figure 1. Panel (a) on the left gives the median length of each kind of query: 16 for human-written, 15 for agent-written, 15 for this paper's generator, and 82 for earlier theorem paraphrases. Panel (b) on the right gives Recall@10 of four retrieval systems on short, ambiguous queries and on long, complete queries: earlier systems all drop markedly on short queries, for example Lean Finder falls from 0.914 to 0.698; Lean Finder V2 scores 0.919 and 0.893, the smallest gap between the two kinds of query.](figs/2610.30843/fig1_ambiguity_gap.png)

The paper gives an example: the target is Mathlib's theorem that "a constant function is even". ## 2. Method

![The overall Lean Finder V2 pipeline (paper Figure 2). ### 2.1 Initial retriever

The retriever starts from Qwen3-Embedding-8B and is fine-tuned with contrastive learning: each query and its theorem form a positive pair, and the other theorems in the same batch are negatives. Many theorems in Mathlib are close to one another, so the authors remove from the negatives any candidate whose cosine similarity exceeds that of the positive by more than a threshold $m$, to avoid penalizing theorems that are in fact also correct. The initial training data are of two kinds, both long queries with full context: synthetic user queries that earlier work summarized from Lean community Zulip discussions, and long natural-language paraphrases of theorems. This step yields the round-0 retriever.

### 2.2 Generating hard queries with reinforcement learning

The query generator is Qwen3-4B, trained with GRPO (a reinforcement learning method that updates the policy by the relative quality of results sampled within the same group). It generates one short query per theorem, with the reward:

$$r=\max\{0,\ j(q,d)\cdot f_{\mathrm{rank}}(k)-\lambda_{\mathrm{len}}\,p_{\mathrm{len}}(L)\}$$

Here $q$ is the generated query, $d$ the theorem, $k$ the rank the current retriever gives the target theorem, and $L$ the query length. The three terms do the following:

- Consistency $j(q,d)$: GPT-OSS-120B judges whether the query and theorem state the same thing; if not, it is 0 and the whole reward goes to zero.
- Difficulty $f_{\mathrm{rank}}(k)$: if the target theorem ranks in the top 5, the query is too easy and scores 0. Between ranks 5 and 30 the reward grows logarithmically with rank, and between ranks 30 and 100 it scores the full 1. Outside the top 100 it scores 0, because that most likely means the query is wrong rather than revealing a weakness of the retriever.
- Length penalty: queries longer than 40 tokens start losing points, reaching the full penalty at 50 tokens, with penalty coefficient $\lambda_{\mathrm{len}}=0.15$. The threshold is based on the length distribution of real queries: the 90th percentiles of human and agent queries are 37 and 28 tokens.

Training also mixes in some supervised fine-tuning whose targets are queries in the real style of how humans and agents search, with the mixing ratio decreasing over training: early on, the supervised signal pins the generator's writing near real queries, and later updates follow mainly the reinforcement learning reward. After each round of generator training, the authors use it to generate more than 300,000 queries for Mathlib theorems and retrain the retriever on them together with the existing long-paraphrase data; the new retriever then provides the ranking reward for the next round. The two alternate for two rounds in total.

On the input side, GEPA optimizes the rewriting prompt. GEPA is a method for automatically revising prompts: a candidate prompt rewrites a small batch of queries, the fixed Lean Finder V2 retriever ranks the target theorems, the prompt is revised based on the ranks and textual feedback, and only versions that improve are kept. Both rewriting and prompt optimization use DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and the queries used for optimization come from the synthetic data of Section 2.2, not the test set.

This experiment checks whether rewriting before retrieval adds further gains. The retriever is fixed to Lean Finder V2, and each rewriting method generates three times. This experiment checks whether both parts of the reward are necessary. The authors change only the reward of the round-1 generator and keep all other settings fixed (paper Table 7, MathlibQR):

- Difficulty reward only: nDCG@1 0.453, below round 0's 0.463.
- Consistency reward only: nDCG@1 0.463, level with round 0, with Recall@10 rising from 0.760 to 0.780.
- Both: nDCG@1 0.520, Recall@10 0.842.

With only the difficulty reward, the generator can worsen the ranking by writing off-target queries, and a retriever trained on such queries learns wrong correspondences. With only the consistency reward, the queries are too easy for the retriever and provide little new information.

The round-2 ablation answers whether more sampling is enough. The authors fix two sampled queries per theorem and the same number of optimization steps, and change only the model that generates the round-2 queries. The paper has no separate limitations section. Two points can be added. First, MathlibQR has only 810 queries, and the real-query evaluation relies on LLM judges; the two judges pick the same top system on 89% of queries, but there are no human-verified rankings. Second, the consistency judgment in the reward is made by GPT-OSS-120B, and its criterion directly decides which kind of "hard" is kept; the paper does not report the error rate of this judgment, and if it is too lenient, off-target queries still slip into the training data.

First, when training a retriever for a specialized domain, first measure the length and phrasing of real queries, then build training data to match that distribution. This paper's data show that the same 8B retriever beats a system with a reranker simply by switching its training data from long paraphrases to short queries close to real lengths.

Second, when synthesizing hard examples with reinforcement learning, a difficulty reward must be paired with a consistency check and a rank cap that gives no reward outside the top 100. The ablation in this paper shows directly that chasing difficulty alone turns synthetic data into noise.

papers.title: CANOPY: Adaptive-Granularity Evidence Compression for Multimodal RAG
papers.authors: Hyojeong Yun, Jueun Kim, Wook-Shin Han
papers.summary: When multimodal RAG compresses retrieved results before handing them to the model, how much to keep cannot be fixed in advance; sometimes a whole table is needed, sometimes one row, sometimes one sentence. CANOPY decides the granularity per item and per question, and cuts the evidence tokens handed to the model by 14.2% to 27.7% at comparable answer accuracy. It organises each retrieved result into nested regions, such as a whole table, a few rows or a single row, and scores each region's relevance to the question with a trained encoder. A smaller region replaces its parent only if it scores at least as high, otherwise the larger context is kept. A separate LLM checks which fact the evidence still lacks and, if one is missing, searches again and compresses the new results the same way. When compressing evidence, how much to keep depends on the question, and sometimes a whole row is more useful than a sentence.
papers.abstract: Multimodal RAG retrieves text, tables, images, and videos, but choosing a retrieval granularity does not determine how much context to retain within each item. Coarse units include irrelevant content, while uniformly fine selection can remove context needed to interpret the evidence. Existing compressors address this trade-off with modality-specific mechanisms, leaving open a shared procedure for adapting the retained extent region by region across heterogeneous items. We introduce CANOPY (Canonical Projection over Hierarchy), a framework for adaptive-granularity post-retrieval evidence compression. CANOPY represents retrieved items as hierarchies and uses a node encoder fine-tuned on gold evidence to score regions against the query. Parent-relative refinement compares these scores to select multiple regions at different granularities without LLM calls for node-level pruning. Because compression cannot recover evidence that was never retrieved, a critic requests targeted follow-up retrieval when it judges the accumulated evidence insufficient; newly retrieved items are compressed before being added. Across five QA benchmarks over a 33M-item heterogeneous corpus, CANOPY achieves higher average answer accuracy than the evaluated retrieval baselines. In the unrouted Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct setting, compression reduces reader-input evidence tokens by 14.2-27.7% relative to the same iterative pipeline without compression, with comparable answer accuracy.

papers.title: From VDBBench to the Top of MMEB: Full-Stack Optimization of Alibaba Cloud AI Search, from Engine to Model
papers.summary: Alibaba Cloud says that after adding FalconSeek, its in-house C++ query kernel, to Elasticsearch, the geometric mean query time on Rally Big5, a set of typical ES queries, got about 6.87 times faster. ES still handles the API, writes and cluster management, and only the most expensive query steps, such as inverted-index traversal, sorting, aggregation and vector recall, run in the C++ kernel, while unsupported queries fall back to the original ES execution. Vector search first finds candidates on the HNSW graph using compressed vectors and then rereads the original vectors to rerank them, handling more than 80 thousand queries per second at about 0.98 recall on a ten-million-vector test set. On the model side, the multimodal document embedding model they open-sourced ranks first on the MMEB VisDoc leaderboard. These are all the vendor's own tests, and the article itself notes that the compared systems ran on different machine specs. ==Search that feeds context to agents needs the engine and the model optimized together==.
papers.abstract: 当 Agent 开始进入生产环境，搜索正在从找到相关文档的工具升级为持续供给高质量上下文的基础设施。AI Search 不再只是搜索引擎，而是贯穿模型理解、向量与全文召回、混合检索、融合重排和引擎执行的完整链路。阿里云 AI Search 在 VDBBench 向量检索、Big5 与 Tantivy 传统检索，以及 MMEB 多模态文档检索等评测中进行全栈优化。

papers.title: Web Search on TokenHub, Tencent Cloud's Model Serving Platform
papers.summary: An LLM's knowledge goes out of date, and questions like what the weather is today require going online. Tencent Cloud's TokenHub turns web search into a tool the model calls itself: once it is switched on, the model decides whether to search and what search terms to write, then builds its answer from the results and marks the cited sources. Developers only choose between the lite and standard versions and how much search content to inject per turn; the model decides how many searches to run. This is a product API document with no evaluation of results.
papers.abstract: 联网搜索是 TokenHub 提供的模型增强能力。开启后，大模型在回答时可自动调用搜索引擎获取实时网络信息，解决模型知识时效性不足的问题。平台支持 Responses API 与 Chat Completions API 两种协议，模型可自主判断是否需要搜索、搜索什么关键词，并基于搜索结果生成回答，同时通过结构化 annotations 返回引用来源。

papers.title: Joint Constraint Aggregation for Qualifier-Sensitive Retrieval-Augmented QA
papers.authors: Jennifer Hsia, Zachary C. Lipton, Aarti Singh
papers.summary: When retrieved passages mention a wrong answer that meets only some of the conditions more often than the right one, the model is easily pulled the wrong way. Checking every candidate against the same set of conditions and then comparing them together sharply reduces this error. On AmbigQA questions where retrieval favours a wrong answer, Qwen3-30B answers 86.4% correctly with step-by-step reasoning and 93.5% with this method. It works in three steps. First the question is broken into conditions every candidate must meet; for a question about which actress said a famous line, the answer must be an actress, not a character she played. Then each candidate is checked against the retrieved passages, with a verdict and a reason for each condition. Finally all candidates' reports are compared side by side and the one that meets every condition is chosen. When a question carries qualifiers, checking each one before comparing is more reliable than answering directly.
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented QA can fail even when the correct answer is in the retrieved evidence. This can happen when a competing answer satisfies some, but not all, of the question's requirements and is mentioned frequently in the retrieved documents, which can make it appear to be the best-supported answer. To test whether this retrieval skew actually affects the decision, we manipulate it directly: increasing the prevalence of passages that favor the competing answer makes the model more likely to select it. This points to a decision problem that candidate-level support alone cannot resolve. We therefore introduce Joint Constraint Aggregation (JCA), which compares candidates against the same question-derived requirements using the retrieved evidence. Across three evaluation settings and three instruction-tuned backbones, JCA improves overall accuracy, and its advantage grows when retrieval favors a competing answer. Together, these results suggest that when partial matches and retrieval prominence pull models toward a competing answer, comparing candidates against the question's full requirements can make selection more reliable.

papers.title: Compiling Autoregressive LLM Control into Policy-Exact Parallel Inference for Hierarchical RAG
papers.authors: Zehao Lin, Qianfeng Shen, Xixuan Hao, Shaobo Cui, Chunyu Li, Kai Chen, Bo Tang, Zhenjun Wang, Jin Yan, Zhiyu Li, Feiyu Xiong
papers.summary: In hierarchical RAG, an LLM picks a few sections from a candidate list to read next, usually by writing out its choice token by token, but the choice can be computed at once. The picked sections almost always match serial decoding, and selection latency falls by 35% to 47%. Each candidate section is bound to a single-token label, and at the position where the next label would be written, the logits of those labels alone give each section's score. One pass over the prompt picks the first section by score. When three sections are picked greedily, once the first is fixed only a few prefixes are ever needed: the one with just the first section, and the first section plus one candidate second section. All these prefixes are packed into one input where each can see only the prompt and its own earlier part. One forward pass gives every section's score under every prefix: the prefix with just the first section yields the second, and the prefix ending in that second section yields the third.
papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly act as controllers in structured decision pipelines, yet their decisions are still executed by autoregressive text decoding. Hierarchical RAG is one such setting: at each frontier of a document tree, an LLM commits to b of k sections under an input-dependent action grammar, executed as either failure-prone free-form JSON or reliable but strictly serial grammar-constrained generation. We show that this serialization is unnecessary for bounded-horizon control: the reachable future forms a shallow action-prefix tree, which we compile—one root prefill plus one tree-causal probe evaluate every prefix-conditioned action distribution with serial decoding's tokens, positions, and causal ancestry. A prefix-state lemma makes compiled control policy-exact in exact arithmetic: the same policy with a two-forward critical path and zero output tokens. One further probe pass certifies the exact order-marginalized MAP set. Across four document-disjoint splits and two scales on the primary MetaX device, compiled control matches the serial policy on 84-89% of questions and cuts control latency by 35-47% versus token-wise serial decoding and 6-7% versus an idealized chunked engine; an H800 repetition preserves the ordering.

papers.title: SurveyGraph: Generating Academic Surveys via Methods-Entity Knowledge Graphs
papers.authors: Yifan Yuan, Yancheng Zhu, Zuoyu Zhang, Xiaogang Peng
papers.summary: When surveys are written automatically, building a graph of which paper extends or improves which, then finding literature along that graph, makes citations better grounded, but the relations in the graph can themselves be wrong. With a graph built from LLM function-calling papers and Qwen writing the survey, the share of cited sentences actually supported by the papers they cite is 2.8 percentage points higher than in a version with the same papers and outline but no graph relations. SurveyGraph links methods, tasks, datasets and other entities into a graph, follows its relations to find related papers for each section, then drafts and revises; relations with too little evidence can be filtered out before retrieval. A human check of 108 relations found only 68.5% fully or partly supported; one claimed that a paper on scientific tool use extends API-Bank, but API-Bank is a benchmark, not an earlier method.
papers.abstract: Most automated survey generation systems retrieve papers as flat documents, limiting their ability to capture research structure. We present SurveyGraph, a framework built around a Methods-Entity Knowledge Graph (MEKG) encoding method-level follow-on, competition, and shared-resource relations. The graph supports core-paper discovery, retrieval, hybrid outlining, and evidence-gated narrative synthesis. We evaluate retrieval, semantic edges, citation grounding, collection coverage, and generation-stage components. In a controlled seven-method equal-budget benchmark, MEKG-anchored fusion balances recall and structural density, with an independent co-citation check. In a separate archived graph-native diagnostic, graph-aware retrieval nearly doubles recall over flat lexical baselines across eight runs (p = 0.004). A semantic evidence gate achieves AUC = 0.75. Audits of 160 generated sentences find 80.6% anchored-or-partial citation support. Human adjudication of 108 stratified semantic edges finds 68.5% supported-or-partial relations. A SurveyBench-facing collection probe reaches mean reference coverage of 0.521 across four topics with an eight-paper budget.

papers.title: Automated Enrichment Analysis with GraphRAG: Efficient Multi-Database ORA Extraction and Biological Interpretation
papers.authors: Guangcan Li, Shuyuan Zheng, Jiayao Liu, Shigeto Seno, Makoto Onizuka
papers.summary: Running enrichment analysis on one knowledge graph built from several gene-set databases gives almost the same results as the standard method, runs much faster, and shows which genes link terms across databases. Enrichment analysis checks whether a set of genes with clearly changed expression falls mostly within a known pathway or functional term, and the standard method runs once per database, producing several unconnected long lists. Here the terms of several databases and the genes they annotate are built into one graph, where shared genes connect terms from different databases. Each term is first scored by whether the changed genes are clearly over-represented in it, then a trade-off between collecting high-scoring terms and adding few edges yields a small subgraph connected through shared genes. High-scoring terms too costly to connect are dropped, and an LLM writes a biological interpretation from the subgraph. On 42 real gene-expression queries, median query time is 37 times faster, and the mean Pearson correlation of term scores with the standard method is 0.997.
papers.abstract: Over-representation analysis (ORA) is widely used to interpret gene-expression studies, but its outputs are often fragmented across gene-set databases and presented as flat term lists that obscure gene-level links among related enrichment signals. We propose Graph-Based Over-Representation Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GBOR-RAG), an integrated and traceable framework for ORA interpretation. GBOR-RAG represents heterogeneous gene-set databases as a unified term-gene knowledge graph, where shared genes connect related terms across sources. After graph-based ORA scoring, the framework retrieves a compact connected evidence subgraph that preserves both cross-database relationships and gene-level support. The subgraph conditions an LLM to generate biological interpretations, and we introduce a claim-level faithfulness metric to assess whether generated claims are supported by explicit evidence. Experiments show that graph-based ORA preserves conventional ORA results with high consistency (mean Pearson r=0.997) while reducing query time by a median of 37x (up to 48x). The retrieved subgraphs average 36.8 nodes and achieve the highest overall integration score (4.12), and GBOR-RAG attains the highest claim-level faithfulness (0.90) among the compared systems. Adding a PubMed literature layer further improves the overall interpretation quality from 4.17 to 4.75.
